summary.text: A 49-year-old married male teacher, HIV-1 positive for eight years and receiving irregular antiretroviral treatment, presented with a painful swelling of the lower third of the right thigh that had appeared three weeks before admission, with intermittent claudication. Examination showed slight fever, right leg cyanosis, a pulsatile necrotic-skinned swelling with a systolic murmur, attenuated pedal pulses, right inguinal lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly.

Workup showed sinus rhythm with polymorphic ventricular extrasystoles, anaemia with haemoglobin 9.6 g/dl, leukoneutropenia, a viral load of 2.5 Log/ml and a CD4 count of 250/mm^(3). Angiography of the lower limbs with IV iodinated contrast revealed a popliteal artery aneurysm with perianeurysmal muscle abscesses. The diagnosis was a right popliteal mycotic aneurysm in pre-rupture complicated by critical limb ischaemia; pathology of the excised mass revealed a eumycetoma.

Surgery consisted of a popliteal aneurysmectomy removing a large cup-shaped spongy mass with 1,800 g of clots, with arterial continuity restored by an interposed inverted saphenous vein graft preceded by ligation of the femorotibial artery ends. The immediate postoperative period was uneventful, with functional recovery allowing return to social and professional activities, and secondary amputation was avoided.
